Bayesian phylogenetic model of the trait gradient, with latent beta

Source: R/trait_gradient_bayes.R
trait_gradient_bayes.Rd

Fits in Stan a bivariate phylogenetic mixed model in which the position of each species along the gradient (\(\beta\)) and its mean trait (\(\bar t\)) are latent species effects, estimated from every site of the species, and returns the phylogenetic signal of \(\beta\), \(\alpha\) and \(\bar t\) with their credible intervals. Unlike trait_gradient_phylo(), which first computes \(\beta\) and then models it with a standard error, here the uncertainty of \(\beta\) enters the model directly.

Usage

trait_gradient_bayes(
  x,
  tree,
  ou_alpha = NULL,
  lambda_prior = c(1, 1),
  chains = 4,
  parallel_chains = 1,
  iter_warmup = 1000,
  iter_sampling = 1000,
  adapt_delta = 0.95,
  seed = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

Result of trait_gradient().

tree

Phylogeny (phylo) with branch lengths; species not in it are left out.

ou_alpha

NULL for Brownian motion, or the strength \(a\) of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, in units of 1 / branch length.

lambda_prior

The two shape parameters of the beta prior of both \(\lambda\).

chains, parallel_chains, iter_warmup, iter_sampling, adapt_delta, seed

Passed to the $sample() method of cmdstanr.

...

Further arguments to $sample(), such as max_treedepth or refresh.

Value

An object of class mc_trait_gradient_bayes, a list with

signal

the phylogenetic share \(\lambda\) of \(\beta\), \(\alpha\) and the mean, and the phylogenetic correlations of \(\beta\) with the mean and with \(\alpha\): estimate (posterior median), lower, upper (95% interval).

variances

the phylogenetic and species variances of the three quantities, in squared trait units.

species

posterior median and 95% interval of \(\beta\), \(\alpha\) and the mean of each species.

diagnostics

largest R-hat, smallest bulk and tail effective sample sizes, number of divergent transitions, and ok.

fit

the CmdStanMCMC object; its draws live in temporary files of the session, so save them with fit$save_object() to keep them.

data, A, ou_alpha, lambda_prior

the data of the model, the phylogenetic correlation matrix and the settings.

Details

Each population (species \(i\) in site \(j\)) contributes two observations: the mean of its site, \(p_{ij}\) (without the focal species, as chosen in trait_gradient()), and its trait value \(t_{ij}\). The model is $$p_{ij} = \mu_p + u^p_i + v^p_i + e^p_{ij}, \qquad t_{ij} = \mu_t + u^t_i + v^t_i + e^t_{ij},$$ where \((u^p, u^t)\) are phylogenetic effects with covariance \(\Sigma_u \otimes A\) (\(A\) the phylogenetic correlation matrix), \((v^p, v^t)\) are species effects without phylogeny with covariance \(\Sigma_v \otimes I\), and the residuals are independent. So \(\beta_i = \mu_p + u^p_i + v^p_i\), \(\bar t_i = \mu_t + u^t_i + v^t_i\) and \(\alpha_i = \bar t_i - \beta_i\), computed for each draw of the posterior.

The variance among species of each response is written as a total, \(\tau^2\), and a phylogenetic share \(\lambda\): \(\sigma_u = \tau \sqrt{\lambda}\) and \(\sigma_v = \tau \sqrt{1 - \lambda}\). \(\lambda\) is between 0 (no phylogenetic signal) and 1 (the structure of A only: Brownian motion, or the OU process given), and its prior is set directly, beta(lambda_prior[1], lambda_prior[2]), uniform by default. (A model with independent priors on \(\sigma_u\) and \(\sigma_v\), as in brms, puts an implicit U-shaped prior on \(\lambda\).) For \(\alpha\), \(\sigma^2_u(\alpha) = \sigma^2_u(t) + \sigma^2_u(p) - 2 \rho_u \sigma_u(t) \sigma_u(p)\), and likewise for \(\sigma^2_v(\alpha)\); its \(\lambda\) follows. The phylogenetic correlation of \(\beta\) with \(\bar t\) is \(\rho_u\), and with \(\alpha\) it follows from the same terms. Both effects are non-centred, so the sampler works when either share is near 0.

With ou_alpha, \(A\) is the correlation matrix of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with strength \(a\) = ou_alpha and a fixed root, as in trait_gradient_phylo(): \(C_{ij} = e^{-a(d_i + d_j - 2 s_{ij})} (1 - e^{-2 a s_{ij}}) / (2a)\), scaled to correlations. \(a\) is taken as known, not estimated: take it from the OU fit of trait_gradient_phylo() for \(\beta\) (response == "beta", model == "OU", column a), which is in the same units. The same \(a\) applies to \(\beta\) and \(\bar t\), because their phylogenetic correlation needs one matrix. As \(a\) goes to 0 the matrix is that of Brownian motion; at large \(a\) it approaches the identity, and the phylogenetic and species effects can no longer be told apart (the function warns). On a tree that is not ultrametric, scaling the Brownian covariance to correlations is not Brownian motion, because the tips have different variances.

Both responses are centred on the mean trait value and divided by its standard deviation, so that \(\alpha\) keeps its meaning, and the results are returned in trait units. Weights (from species_weights in trait_gradient()) multiply the log-likelihood of each population and are divided by their mean, so that they change the relative influence of populations without changing their number. A weighted observation then counts as that many full observations, so unequal weights, such as abundances, make the posterior too narrow: the effective sample is \((\sum w)^2 / \sum w^2\) rather than the number of populations. The function warns when this is below 70% of the populations; species_weights = "occurrence" avoids the problem.

Priors, on the standardised scale: normal(0, 1) for the intercepts, exponential(1) for the total standard deviations among species and for the residuals, beta(1, 1) for both \(\lambda\) (change with lambda_prior), and lkj(2) for the two correlations. Check convergence (diagnostics: R-hat below 1.01, bulk and tail effective sample sizes above 400 and no divergent transitions, over the intercepts, standard deviations, \(\lambda\), correlations, species values and lp__) and the fit, with bayesplot::pp_check() on the result, before reading the estimates.

The model is in system.file("stan", "trait_gradient.stan", package = "comdynamite"). It is compiled by cmdstanr the first time it is used and kept in tools::R_user_dir("comdynamite", "cache"). The pointwise log-likelihoods are in log_lik_p (site means) and log_lik_t (trait values): cross-validation, for instance to compare values of ou_alpha, needs one response at a time, fit$loo(variables = "log_lik_p"), because the two responses are fitted to different sets of populations.

Limits

The phylogenetic part is Brownian motion or an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with a given strength, shared by both responses; trait_gradient_phylo() estimates the strength. Site means of species that share a site are almost the same number, but the model treats them as independent observations, so the posterior of \(\beta\) is somewhat too narrow when species share many sites. The site mean of a population also contains the trait values of the species it lives with, so when relatives co-occur, the phylogenetic correlation \(\rho_u\) of \(\beta\) and \(\bar t\) is inflated by their shared values, not only by niche conservatism. The residuals of the two responses are taken as independent, which ignores the slope of the trait on the gradient within species; trait_gradient() estimates those slopes. Sites where a species is the only species have no site mean without it and enter only its trait; a species that is alone in all its sites has no data on \(\beta\), and its \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\) are returned as NA.

Splitting the variance among species into a phylogenetic and a non-phylogenetic part needs many species, and the intervals of \(\lambda\) stay wide. In 60 trials with 40–45 species, 30 sites, occurrence weights and the default settings, where the niches evolved with Pagel's \(\lambda\) of 0, 0.5 or 1 (20 trials each):

\(\lambda = 0\)\(\lambda = 0.5\)\(\lambda = 1\)
median of \(\lambda_\beta\) (range of the 20 medians)0.07 (0.05–0.31)0.24 (0.04–0.73)0.94 (0.38–0.99)
95\ lower bound above 0.05 / upper bound below 0.950 / 205 / 2016 / 1
passed every diagnostic12118

A fit took 9–30 s with four chains in parallel. One of the 60 fits had a divergent transition; the fits that failed the diagnostics did so by an effective sample size below 400 or an R-hat between 1.01 and 1.03, for which longer chains (iter_sampling) are the first remedy (not tested here). Intermediate signal is estimated low (interpretation: the \(\lambda\) of \(\beta\) is below that of the niches, because \(\beta\) also carries the error of the site means), and its interval rarely excludes 0: a wide interval for \(\lambda_\beta\) means that the data do not tell. An earlier version of this model fitted with brms, with independent priors on the two standard deviations, had divergent transitions in most fits and pulled intermediate signal to 0 (median 0.04, interval containing 0.5 in 12 of the same 20 trials). In trials with 18 species the chains of that version did not mix. Use trait_gradient_phylo() to test the signal as well, and do not read a fit that fails diagnostics.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # interactive() && requireNamespace("cmdstanr", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("treeshapesim", quietly = TRUE)
set.seed(1)
tree <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(40)
sim <- simulate_metacommunity(landscape_implicit(30), species_traits(tree, lambda = 1),
                              competition_matrix(tree, "none"), n_steps = 100,
                              seed_steps = 1:5)
ind <- sample_individuals(sim, n = 5, local_adaptation = 0.5, intraspecific_sd = 1)
tg <- trait_gradient(ind, abundance = "abundance", species_weights = "occurrence")
bayes <- trait_gradient_bayes(tg, tree, parallel_chains = 4)
bayes$diagnostics
bayes$signal
bayesplot::pp_check(bayes, resp = "sitemean")
}
